catalog_locator: Ogunmodimu 2015, ch. 2 'The Phonology of Ahan', §2.4 'Tones', body pp. 33-34 (rendered and); parallel statement §1.3.2 'Tone', body p. 12 (scan); §2.3 syllable structure body p. 33; §2.5 phonological processes body p. 34.
catalog_quote: [§2.4 Tones, pp. 33-34] Ahan is a tone language with three phonemic principal tonal patterns – the high [´], mid (which is not marked orthographically) and the low [`]. Tones in Ahan perform lexical functions as contrastive pitches differentiate lexical items in meaning as demonstrated in the example below. a. [ùgbà] ‘time’ b. [ugbà] ‘climbing rope’ c. [ùgbá] ‘garden egg’. Tones in Ahan perform lexical functions; we do not observe any obvious syntactic function perform by tones. [§2.5, p. 34] Àhàn is a language that sticks more to faithfulness of input and output and as such, it does not attest deletion and assimilation. This is one area where is different from the Standard Yoruba and other Yoruboid languages. [§1.3.2 Tone, p. 12] Like many other West African languages, Ahan is a tone language with three phonemic principal tonal patterns tagged the high [A], mid [A] and low [A]. The distribution and the realization of tonemes in Ahan is a major component of this research.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (271 pp, EPSON scan, no text) and rendered pp. 1, 30, 51, 52 as images to read them directly. The quoted passage is on pp. 51-52 = printed body pp. 33-34, section 2.4 Tones, exactly as the compiler gives it, with one class of difference: the scanned dropped the tone diacritics. The printed text reads "Ahan is a tone language with three phonemic principal tonal patterns - the high [´], mid [] (which is not marked orthographically) and the low [`]." and the minimal set is a. [ùgbà] 'time', b. [ugbà] 'climbing rope', c. [ùgbá] 'garden egg', followed by "Tones in Ahan perform lexical functions; we do not observe any obvious syntactic function perform by tones." the compiler file locator…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement on word stress or accent anywhere in the grammar (scanned of all 271 pages, 0 hits for 'stress'; 6 hits for 'accent' are all about English/German pitch accent focus marking in §6.2.1, not Ahan). The phonology chapter describes Àhàn as a three-tone (H/M/L) language with lexically contrastive tone; syllables are V or CV, no codas. Stress is simply not mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only prosodic remarks concern tone: tone stays on the surviving vowel under (restricted V+N) vowel elision ('tonal stability'), N+N elision and assimilation are not attested, and English loans are re-toned via the Ekiti dialect.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone, illustrated with isolated citation forms ([ugba] minimal set); no phrase-level stress or intonation discussion for Àhàn. Tone diacritics on the [ugba] examples were lost in scanned (the PDF is image-only).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the single Àhàn variety spoken in the Ahan quarter of Òmùò-Èkìtì (Ekiti State); no dialects are distinguished. Ogunmodimu 2015 treats it as a Defoid/Yoruboid-adjacent language distinct from Yoruba; Akanbi 2014/2015 place it in an 'Ahanoid' group with Àyèré. This is Glottolog ahan1244 = ISO ahn; no differently named variety involved.

sources.note: Nothing about stress in the whole dissertation (image-only PDF; scanned all 271 pp at 150 dpi, one tesseract at a time; 0 hits for 'stress'). Ch. 2 (pp. 23-42) describes consonants, oral/nasal vowels, V/CV syllable structure with no codas, three lexical tones H/M/L ('we do not observe any obvious syntactic function perform by tones'), restricted V+N vowel elision with tonal stability, no assimilation, vowel epenthesis in loans.
